summary: This standards-track memo defines the command codes and attributes (AVPs) needed to carry EAP packets between a network access server and a back-end authentication server using Diameter. This lets a network access server pass EAP authentication on to a central server.

plainLanguage.summary: The Diameter EAP application lets a Network Access Server pass EAP authentication messages to a back-end server. The server makes the authentication decision and returns a result for the NAS to apply.

subtitle: How a Network Access Server relays EAP authentication to a back-end Diameter server.

tldr.problem: A Network Access Server often acts only as an EAP pass-through and needs a standard way to send authentication packets to a back-end server.
tldr.mechanism: The Diameter EAP application defines request and answer commands plus AVPs for carrying EAP packets, results, and optional keying material between the NAS and server.
tldr.outcome: The application lets a NAS relay EAP exchanges and defines rules for errors, retransmission, accounting, and RADIUS translation. RFC 4072 was updated by RFC 7268 and RFC 8044.

today: RFC 4072 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 7268 and RFC 8044. Read both updates with this application specification.

sections.title: Carrying EAP through Diameter
sections.content:
The Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) supports multiple authentication methods over different kinds of links. This RFC defines the Diameter EAP application, which carries EAP packets between a Network Access Server (NAS) acting as an authenticator and a back-end authentication server.

Authentication takes place between the EAP client and its home Diameter server. The application builds on Diameter's Network Access Server application and can be used alongside it. It also defines commands and Attribute-Value Pairs (AVPs) and can interoperate with RADIUS EAP support.
sections.plainLanguage: The NAS carries EAP messages between a user and a back-end server. The server checks the authentication exchange and tells the NAS whether it succeeded.

sections.title: How the EAP Exchange Proceeds
sections.content:
Diameter nodes advertise the EAP application with Application ID 5. Once EAP starts on the link, the NAS typically sends a Diameter-EAP-Request with an empty EAP-Payload to signal EAP-Start. The server replies with an EAP request and a result indicating that another round is expected.

The NAS passes the server's EAP request to the client and sends the client's response back to the server in another request. The exchange can continue for multiple rounds. A preferred approach is for the NAS to send an EAP-Request/Identity itself and forward the client's identity response in the first Diameter request, reducing Diameter round trips.

The final Diameter answer reports success or failure. The NAS uses the Diameter Result-Code to decide whether to provide service and must not make that decision from the optional EAP payload. A successful answer may include authorization AVPs and an EAP-Master-Session-Key.
sections.plainLanguage: The NAS passes questions to the user and answers back to the server. When the exchange ends, the NAS follows the server's Diameter result to decide whether to provide service.

sections.title: Ways to Connect the NAS and Server
sections.content:
The RFC describes four example arrangements for protecting and routing Diameter messages that may carry an EAP master session key. They are not an exhaustive list and can be combined. Diameter's IPsec and TLS protect messages hop by hop; the document says no end-to-end NAS-to-home-server security mechanism is defined there.

  • The NAS can connect directly to the home server, which provides authorization data and keying material.
  • A redirect agent can tell the NAS which home server to contact.
  • The home server can perform EAP authentication while local proxy agents provide authorization AVPs in a separate NASREQ exchange.
  • Proxy agents can relay the exchange, but can see EAP session keys.

The proxy arrangement is unsuitable when those agents cannot be trusted with the keys.
sections.plainLanguage: The NAS may contact the home server directly or use redirect and proxy agents. Any agent in the path can see the keying material described by the RFC, so it must be trusted.

sections.title: Diameter-EAP Request and Answer
sections.content:
The Diameter-EAP-Request (DER) and Diameter-EAP-Answer (DEA) share Command-Code 268. A DER travels from the Diameter client to the server and carries an EAP response in one EAP-Payload AVP. The payload may be empty to begin an EAP session. Later DER messages must repeat State AVPs carried in the preceding answer.

A DEA travels back from the server. It either requests another round, reports successful authentication and authorization, or reports failure. A successful result must cause the access device to provide service. If authorization was requested, the successful answer must include the relevant authorization AVPs.

The messages also carry required session and application information and may carry other NASREQ AVPs. The RFC assigns codes to EAP-Payload, EAP-Reissued-Payload, EAP-Master-Session-Key, and Accounting-EAP-Auth-Method.
sections.plainLanguage: A DER carries an EAP response from the NAS to the server. A DEA carries the server's next question or final result back to the NAS.

sections.title: AVPs for EAP Data and Accounting
sections.content:
An AVP is a named field in a Diameter message. EAP-Payload carries the EAP packet. EAP-Reissued-Payload carries a previous EAP request after a non-fatal error. EAP-Master-Session-Key carries keying material used to protect communication between the user and NAS; how it is used depends on the link layer and is outside this RFC.

Accounting-EAP-Auth-Method identifies the EAP method used. The EAP-Key-Name attribute carries an opaque identifier generated by an EAP method. A NAS sends that attribute empty in a request, and a server silently discards it if it contains data.

Accounting messages may include the authentication method and the EAP method used. The RFC also specifies which AVPs may appear in the request, answer, and accounting messages.
sections.plainLanguage: The added AVPs carry EAP packets, a prior request, keying material, or the name of the authentication method. Accounting can record which EAP method was used.

sections.title: Invalid Packets and Retransmission
sections.content:
The NAS must check EAP packet Code, Identifier, and Length fields before forwarding packets. It checks that client responses match the current request identifier and discards responses that do not match. The NAS may not validate EAP method fields, so an invalid packet can still pass through.

If a server cannot understand an EAP payload, it decides whether the error is fatal based on the EAP type. For a non-fatal error, it sends a multi-round answer with no EAP-Payload and includes the previous request in EAP-Reissued-Payload. The NAS retries with an available response or resends the previous request.

The NAS retransmits EAP packets that are lost between it and the client. The server can set the timer for a request with Multi-Round-Time-Out. A NAS may provide Framed-MTU so the server does not send an EAP payload that exceeds the link's size limit.
sections.plainLanguage: The NAS checks packet headers and discards responses with the wrong identifier. When packets are lost, it can resend them; the server can also set how long the NAS waits for a reply.

sections.title: Translating Between Diameter and RADIUS
sections.content:
Translation agents can carry EAP exchanges between Diameter and RADIUS, following the general NASREQ translation guidance. One or more RADIUS EAP-Message attributes become a single Diameter EAP-Payload AVP; an empty attribute signals EAP-Start. In the reverse direction, a Diameter EAP-Payload may be split across multiple RADIUS EAP-Message attributes.

An EAP-Reissued-Payload maps to RADIUS EAP-Message attributes with Error-Cause value 202. Multi-Round-Time-Out maps to RADIUS Session-Timeout. The EAP-Master-Session-Key may map to the RADIUS MS-MPPE-Recv-Key and MS-MPPE-Send-Key attributes.

Accounting-EAP-Auth-Method maps to the vendor-specific MS-Acct-EAP-Type attribute. That RADIUS attribute cannot represent expanded EAP types, so values greater than 255 should be translated to 254.
sections.plainLanguage: A translation agent rewrites EAP fields when a message crosses between Diameter and RADIUS. The two protocols can carry the same exchange, but some accounting values have different limits.

sections.title: Security and Trust Between Nodes
sections.content:
IPsec or TLS can protect Diameter messages between neighboring nodes. Nodes also need to authorize which servers may act for a realm and which clients may act as a NAS. Redirects make this especially important because a compromised agent could supply an incorrect home-server address.

Proxy agents can alter results or authorization AVPs, and they can see the EAP master session key. The RFC strongly recommends avoiding agents that cannot be trusted to keep keys secret. Per-connection and per-user policy can reduce attacks that try to downgrade authentication to PAP or CHAP.

Messages may reveal user identity and approximate location. Identity-protecting EAP methods and pseudonyms can reduce that exposure. A compromised NAS can also give the client a false description of the network even if it possesses the required keys.
sections.plainLanguage: Every Diameter peer and proxy must be trusted and authorized, because an agent can change results or see keying material. Authentication messages can also reveal identity and location information.
